meta.name: Agent fleet
meta.summary: An always-on fleet of agents that turns a written order into a reviewed slice, with a human at the plan and again at the merge.

story.headline: How much of the work can leave your hands before it stops being reviewable?
story.problem: Agent sessions forget themselves. A plan, the reason a decision was made, the test that proved it, the one that failed twice: all of it dies with the context window. Multi-step work needs somewhere durable to live, and a gate that an operator at 1am cannot skip by accident. The alternative is either no delegation or delegation nobody can audit.
story.approach: Work arrives as an issue rather than a chat message, so it survives a lost session. A label decides which machine picks it up. An orchestrator reads a frozen brief and decomposes it into tasks; an implementer runs one task at a time in a throwaway checkout and escalates after two failures instead of grinding. Every task leaves evidence the orchestrator must read before the next one starts. Nothing merges on an agent's word: the plan and the merge each need an explicit human reply.
story.outcome: The pipeline has shipped 22 slice units on this site, each through the same two gates. Fifteen revisions were logged and coded by cause rather than by blame, and each one changed the brief or the template that produced the next slice. Seven CI contexts must pass before a merge is even offered.

layers.name: Human surface
layers.description: The two places where a person is required, and the record that makes them meaningful.

components.name: Chat surface
components.description: A written request lands in a channel, not in a terminal. Threads keep the request, the links and the replies together, so the order can be read back weeks later by someone who was not there.

components.name: Approval gate
components.description: The plan needs a human word before implementation starts, and the merge needs another before anything reaches the main branch. The gate is deliberate friction: it is the one place where a plausible-looking failure gets caught before it becomes history.

components.name: Review thread
components.description: Each slice keeps one thread: the handoff, the verdict, any objection, and the evidence linked from it. A decision that only exists in a chat log is a rumour; a decision with a thread is a record.

layers.name: Intake
layers.description: How an instruction becomes durable work, and how it is routed without a scheduler guessing.

components.name: Issue intake
components.summary: An order that survives the session
components.description: Every request is written as an issue with a body: scope, acceptance, what not to touch. The issue is the unit that survives a lost session, a restarted host or a change of model behind the seat.

components.name: Label router
components.summary: Routing by label, not by guess
components.description: A label on the issue decides which machine picks the work up. Routing is a declaration, not an inference: if the work lands on the wrong host, the label was wrong and that is visible in one glance.

components.name: Dedup state
components.description: Recurring jobs and repeated requests consult a small state file before they speak. Without it the fleet is a machine for saying the same thing twice, which trains the operator to ignore it.

layers.name: Execution
layers.description: One slice at a time: plan, implement, prove, judge. Each step leaves something the next one can check.

components.name: Orchestrator
components.description: Reads the frozen brief, decomposes it into tasks, dispatches them and reviews what comes back. It does not implement: the seat that plans is not the seat that types, so a plan cannot quietly become whatever the code did.

components.name: Implementer
components.description: Takes a single task, works in its own checkout, runs the tests and reports. Two failed attempts escalate to the orchestrator instead of a third guess; the cost of a wrong turn is bounded by design.

components.name: Worktree
components.description: Each task runs against its own working copy. Parallel work cannot collide, and a run that goes wrong is discarded by deleting a directory rather than by untangling a branch.

components.name: Evidence
components.description: Logs, screenshots, measured numbers and a self-check that maps every acceptance criterion to the artefact that proves it. A task is not done because the implementer says so; it is done when the criterion has a file behind it.

components.name: Gate check
components.description: Acceptance is a test result, not an opinion. When a criterion turns out to be unmeetable, the criterion is revised in daylight and logged with its cause; it is never quietly reinterpreted to fit what was built.

layers.name: Fleet
layers.description: Two machines and a clock: long-lived work on one, hands-on work on the other.

components.name: Edge host
components.description: The long-lived machine: queue watchers, scheduled jobs, backups, and the agent that talks to the operator. It holds little state of its own — what matters lives in the vault and the queue.

components.name: Workstation
components.description: The second machine holds the editor seats and does the heavy local builds. Splitting the fleet this way keeps interactive work from competing with always-on watchers for the same machine.

components.name: Cron
components.description: Scheduled upkeep: digests, backups, health checks, capacity watchdogs. Each job carries its own time budget and is killed when it overruns, because an unattended job that can hang is a silent outage with a schedule.

flows.label: An order comes in
flows.description: A written request becomes an issue, a label routes it to a machine, and the orchestrator turns the frozen brief into tasks that the implementer runs one at a time.

flows.label: A slice goes out
flows.description: The task's evidence is checked against the criterion, the slice is reviewed in its thread, and nothing merges until a human says the word.

flows.label: Nightly upkeep
flows.description: Scheduled jobs wake the edge host, spend their budget and exit; their results land where the next morning's digest can find them.
